desc:
The depth of a node is the number of edges on the path from the root to that node, so the root has depth 0, its children have depth 1, and so on.

Return the sum of the depths of all nodes in the tree. The empty tree gives 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 9, 20, -1, -1, 15, 7] the depths are 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, so the answer is 6.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Compute the depth of each node and add them up. The depth of a node is one more than the depth of its parent.
You do not need recursion or a separate traversal order: process the nodes so that every parent is handled before its children.
In the level-order array the parent always appears before its children. One left-to-right pass can set depth[child] = depth[parent] + 1 while adding to the sum.
editorial: A parent is always processed before its children in level order, so the depth of every node can be derived in O(1) from its parent's depth. Keep the running sum while assigning depths.

A recursive version passes the current depth down: f(node, d) = d + f(left, d + 1) + f(right, d + 1). Both are linear. The answer can reach about 1.1 million on a path of 1,500 nodes, comfortably inside 32-bit integers.
